title: Posner Spatial Cueing
summary: Run a spatial-cueing experiment on yourself. Compare valid, neutral and invalid trials to separate the benefit of a valid cue from the cost of an invalid one.
learningObjectives: Describe the spatial-cueing paradigm and the role of valid, neutral and invalid trials.
Separate a benefit of valid cueing from a cost of invalid cueing using a neutral baseline.
Explain why a valid-minus-invalid difference conceals which of the two produced it.
Distinguish covert orienting from overt eye movements, and say what evidence would be needed to tell them apart.
Recognise browser reaction times, anticipation cut-offs and small cell sizes as limits on what a classroom block can show.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; trials are timed and summarised in the browser tab only, nothing survives a reset, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: No trial is ever timed out - the target persists until answered, nothing animates and nothing flashes, so there is no flicker for a photosensitive reader to encounter and no motion for a reduced-motion rule to switch off. Six untimed practice trials with explanatory feedback run first, and the key mapping is stated before anything begins. Responses accept the Left and Right arrow keys or two buttons at least 3.5rem tall. The cue is carried by three things at once - a much heavier border, the accent colour, and a caret glyph under the box - so it is legible in greyscale and in forced colours. A complete non-timed route exists and is signposted before the task: the seeded worked example fills the same results panel and reaches every conclusion without performing the experiment, which also serves readers for whom the visual display is not usable. The trial display is aria-hidden during a run because a spoken description of a 400 ms cue would arrive after the trial had ended. Charts are hidden from assistive technology and paired with a visible table carrying the same numbers; every control has an accessible name; headings do not skip; focus moves to the results heading when a block ends. Usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths with no horizontal page scroll.
readmeTopic: Spatial cueing: separating the benefit of a valid cue from the cost of an invalid one
simulationNotes: The learner's own block is real timing from their own responses, but in a browser tab: display refresh, keyboard latency and background load add tens of milliseconds, so the numbers are illustrative rather than psychophysical. Responses under 150 ms are treated as anticipations and responses over 2000 ms as lapses; both are counted, reported and excluded from the means. Only correct trials contribute to condition means. The worked example is generated by RT = 340 + condition offset + Normal(0, 45) + Exponential(mean 35), with offsets of -28 for valid, 0 for neutral and +52 for invalid, and accuracies of .98, .97 and .94; n = 96 (48 valid, 32 neutral, 16 invalid) with fixed seed 20260823, so it is identical on every press. It produces valid 348 ms, neutral 374 ms, invalid 440 ms - a benefit of 26 ms and a cost of 66 ms. Those parameters were chosen to make both halves legible with the cost the larger, as it usually is in the literature. They are not a norm, not a published effect size and not anybody's data. The page cannot measure eye position, so nothing here demonstrates covert orienting rather than an unnoticed eye movement, and it says so in the hero panel, the debrief and the teaching notes.
